utterances.text: In paragraph 55, it says that: "Forces of the FRY and Serbia, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic manner, forcibly expelled and internally displaced hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians from their homes across the entire province of Kosovo ... by creating an atmosphere of fear and oppression through the use of force, threats of force, and acts of violence." Tell me loud and clear, did you create an atmosphere of fear? Did you threaten Albanians or use acts of violence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: This is certainly not true. At that time, on the eve of the aggression, the army had many serious tasks facing it. It was with the beginning of the NATO aggression that fighting started with terrorists and our forces, so that our army and the police had the responsibility and the duty to fight simultaneously against NATO aggression on the one hand and against terrorists on the other hand. The terrorists who, with the NATO aggression, received full fire support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph 63, it says, among other things, that in certain cases people were killed, many were threatened with being killed, and many businesses belonging to Albanians were torched while the businesses of Serbs were protected. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Many businesses were set on fire belonging both to Serbs and Albanians, but those fires were caused by NATO bombs. It is understandable that many more Albanian businesses were hit because there were simply many more Albanian businesses than Serb businesses, but that depends entirely on the ratio of these two ethnic groups, their representation in the total population. But one thing that is certain is that it was not done by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said the main reason why people fled was the activity of NATO Air Force. Do we have in tab 3 an overview of actions performed by the NATO Air Force?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this map please be placed on that board, because the general explained that he was responsible for the entire airspace of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Show us, please, what you said on the map.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: This map -- I can't hear. This map shows the deployment of units of the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade of the air defence in two periods. The first period is up to the 9th of April, 1999. We see that here. They are deployed mainly in the area of Djakovica. After that, and that is after the attack on Kosare, from the moment when ground invasion became a certainty, my units were here as well as the supporting units of air defence. The 52nd Brigade was not the only one responsible in Kosovo and Metohija for air defence, but in the Pristina Corps it was the only air defence brigade. This is where the 52nd Brigade was until the 9th of April and after that. After the 9th of April, one artillery battalion, the 3rd Battalion, was in Bec. The 1st Artillery Battalion was in Kijevo. The 4th artillery battalion was in the area of Pristina, Gracanica; and the 2nd Artillery Battalion was in the area of Gnjilane. Pursuant to a decision by the corps commander, they were deployed in such a way as to be able to defend all the most important elements of the disposition of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question that was asked was whether this map represented an overview of the activities of NATO. Now, you don't seem to be dealing -- so the map doesn't do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you were asked was whether this map showed an overview of the bombing activities of NATO. Does it show that? Because that's not what your answer has dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer was an attempt to show the disposition of troops, and I was intending to deal with the bombing activities of NATO when I continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. General, look at this map which is an overview of the activities of the NATO Air Force. Could you please place this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- on the board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we take it the one that's up there is not an overview of the activities of NATO and that we've just wasted five minutes on that question? Because that's what I've been looking for on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain. This is the map, but in this case we see this overview in table form and a specific display deals only with Djakovica because Djakovica was the base for myself and my units. For the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, we have another map where it is shown in detail. What we see on this one is the number of sorties, the type of attacks, the number of planes involved, the increase of activities with time and the losses incurred as well as the bombs used. But we have another map that shows in greater detail certain events, certain incidents in actual places, individual places in Kosovo and Metohija. Bombing activities concerning Djakovica can be shown on this map, whereas the next map can be used for the rest of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with the preparation of this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When -- when was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the map I prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was it prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime in the last month, based on reports and documents that are contemporaneous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how did you get access to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the aggression ended, we made all sorts of analyses and a lot has been published about the NATO aggression. A war report was published and there were also, while it lasted, daily press conferences with detailed explanations given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please listen to the questions I'm asking you and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. answer the questions. How did you get access to the contemporaneous documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of the access that I had I got through Mr. Milosevic's lawyers, but I also had access to public records, public reports, analyses that were made, and finally, we had a report that was the work product of the commission that analysed the effects of the NATO aggression against the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is that commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a commission of the Office of the Prosecutor that reviewed the lawsuit filed by the FRY concerning the NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A commission of the office of which Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you used that report as a partial basis for this -- for this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this other map be placed on the overhead projector now, please. On the board, not on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that tab 46?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 46, yes, tab 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, does this map show -- or, rather, not to put the question that way. Tell me what the map shows. What does the map show, and what is designated on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: On this map -- this map shows the places where the NATO airstrikes took place, the targets of the NATO airstrikes, which means this is not the number of projectiles, this is not the number of bombs, this is the number of attacks on individual places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's not numbers, it's places.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, places targeted by the NATO Air Force. For example, on Pristina. There were 460 attacks launched on Pristina, and on a map of this kind you couldn't put 460 triangles. The number of operations and the number of lethal weapons expulsed is impossible to show in graphic form in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Let's just clear one point up: The triangles indicate the places which were targeted by the NATO Air Force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And does it also indicate the places where -- that were actually bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't hear your question properly. I couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not the places that were targeted but places that were actually bombed by NATO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They are places where the bombs or rockets fell. They are places that were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Thanks to Mr. Robinson's explanation, or the explanation you gave him, those were places where NATO projectiles fell; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, projectiles or bombs or tank cannon balls and so forth, targeted by the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, since we're dealing with this topic and you explained that the refugees or, rather, that the population fled because of the bombing, I'm going to ask you now, bearing in mind the fact that in paragraph 63.1 speaks of alleged deportations performed by our forces, carried out by our forces, I am going to quote the places in their order, and I'd like to ask you to point to their location on the map, the ones I'm going to read out, and tell us whether the bombs fell on those places.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Point A or, rather, paragraph 63(a) is Orahovac. Show us where Orahovac lies.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, paragraph 63(b) mentions another place, and that is Prizren. Show us the Prizren area, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 63(c) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I consider this very important. Can you direct us as to the dates when these places were bombed and the -- so that I can try to relate it to the dates of the alleged flights of the people from those areas. Because your case, as I understand it, is that the people fled following the bombing, or are you also saying that some of the flights also took place simply in anticipation of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, homo sapiens, once the bombing starts, you can flee from bombs that have not landed on your head. If they -- you have been hit by bombs, you cannot flee. So I wanted us to take a look at all the places, all the different places mentioned in paragraph 63 relating to deportation, under the heading of deportation, so that you can see how many places there were in those localities where the bombs fell. For example, in the example of Orahovac and Prizren, another case in point, that was where the bombing was most dense. And we'll look at it date-wise, too, because it says from the 24th of March to the 12th of May, and in Pristina there were 409 attacks, as the general said. Whether 409 attacks took place in the same area, certainly not, but in the general Pristina area there were 409 sorties or attacks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... find out as to whether the witness can help us as to the dates when the bombings took place in these villages where there were flights. So let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you showed us Orahovac. According to that map of yours, were there many places in that area that were bombed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Prizren? You indicated Prizren to us. Were there many places bombed there too?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, there were 326 places that were bombed in the general Prizren area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, paragraph 63(c) mentioned Srbica. Show us Srbica on the map. And that's where there was a lot of bombing, too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 63(d), Suva Reka. Indicate Suva Reka to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Suva Reka is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 63(e) is Pec. Show us Pec, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 63(f), Kosovska Mitrovica, point that out to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 63(g) is Pristina. Show us that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 63(h) is Djakovica. Show us Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 63(i) is Gnjilane. Point to Gnjilane, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 63(j) is Urosevac. Show us Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 63(k) is Kacanik. Point to Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That same paragraph, paragraph 63(l), is Decani. Point to Decani for us.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 63(m) is Vucitrn. Show us Vucitrn, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that completes the list of locations under the heading of "Deportation." Now, all the places that you have indicated, were they the target of intensive bombing and is that where there was a high bombardment density?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. I have drawn up a more detailed map according to the different bombing periods for each month, month by month. I think that you have that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope I've found it. I hope I can find it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Anyway, it indicates monthly periods and the exact points month-by-month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. We'll deal with that in due course. But anyway, we've gone through all the places mentioned in this paragraph, all the letters, the paragraphs -- subparagraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it would appear that our forces have been accused of deportation precisely from places which were most bombed. Where there was no bombing, there doesn't seem to be any charges or accusations of deportation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. I've switched it on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, this map, does it show the targets of NATO attacking Kosovo and Metohija and could give us additional explanation; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this next map be placed on the board, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not clear to me whether this is a tabbed map or not. I'm not sure if the accused would -- perhaps the accused would make it clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a map which is an addition to the map with the dates; is that right? It's a supplement.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's a map that was drawn up, as far as I understood it -- well, it was brought in yesterday because it just defines the map we've seen more precisely according to date.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: What we can see here is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This shows it in greater detail, the periods and the different targets in Kosovo and Metohija. I have taken three periods on this particular map. Had we taken every day, looked at it every day, we wouldn't have been able to record all the actions on the many locations. For example, this colour here, the orange colour, shows the operations in the first month of the NATO aggression, from the 24th of March, that is, until the 25th of May. And this is where it started; Djakovica, Pristina. All the places were bombed. All these places were bombed both in the first month and later on throughout. The red, the red colour, indicates the operations and targeting for Easter, the greatest Orthodox religious holiday, Easter. The operations were launched against Djakovica, Pristina, the orange here again, and the bombing of Klina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And other places in mauve, in purple. Now, general, you said a moment ago that the orange denotes the first month and then you said from March to May. Is that a mistake or what?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: From the 24th of March until the 25th of April is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes. I assumed that there was an error there because you said the first month and then you said May, whereas it was April.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Now, the blue, the blue colour takes us from the 25th of April to the 25th of May. They are operations against these blue areas. And the next period is from the 25th of May to the end of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: And this also indicates places where depleted uranium was used in the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What colour denotes depleted uranium? I wasn't able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Well, operations of bombing with depleted uranium are --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I asked what you colour on the map shows you this.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Oh, it is this sign here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. This circle with the dots.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, the circle with the dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is deleted uranium, when deleted uranium was used; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. The number of charges hasn't been shown because there are 300 and upwards. So it is impossible to count them all because there were almost 200 to 300 charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Charged from where?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: From a cannon, a seven-barrel cannon and a high velocity cannon. That is to say the seven-barrelled cannon is the highest velocity of cannon. And in the squares, the squares shows characteristic targets where civilians were killed, is a representative example. Like Luzane, a bus with civilians in Kulina next to Rozaje; Meja, the refugee settlement at Meja, or rather, the column of refugees in Meja on the 14th of April. And further on, another attack here on a refugee Serb settlement from Krajina, Maja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Point that out on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Here it is. That is Bistrazin, the Maja settlement. It is a refugee settlement. This is Meja, the place where they targeted Siptar refugees for the first time. This is a place called Luzane, where a bus was hit with passengers in it, a civilian coach with passengers. And this is another place here, Sabina Vode [phoen] or Kulina, where a bus was hit with passengers from Metohija on their way to Montenegro. And here we have how many civilians were killed, the figures of how many civilians were killed in Kosovo and Metohija by NATO bombing. How many were killed on the roads and how many were killed in settlements. This, of course, does not include the casualties and the victims that were found underneath the rubble and ruins of buildings and features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you by any chance know the book titled "NATO Crimes in Yugoslavia, Documentary Evidence," which was published by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of your country?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: I've seen the book, some of it. I haven't read it in detail, just in part, but I have other information and sources because I used sources first of all on the basis of regular daily press conferences that took place parallel to the bombardment. Whenever there was a bombardment, there would be a press conference held in Pristina or Belgrade, one of the press centres in those places, but yes, I have seen the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you're saying now should have been contained in those books.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In those books, yes, but also we have more specific concrete data. I have concrete data for Djakovica, for instance, on the basis of combat -- the combat diary of one of the commanders of the battalion, and this reflects the situation exactly. This map does not contain it all. There were many situations where the communication lines were interrupted and we in Djakovica were not able to inform our superiors in Pristina about what was going on about the bombardment for them to be able to state that at the press conferences that they gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this isn't final the number either, the final count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, those -- those books are tabs 28 and 29 of D275, which is marked for identification pending translation. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, all the books were given in the English language, because the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia gave those six, or was it seven, white books. They were all published in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I remember. I was mistaken in terms of the reason why it was put -- marked for identification. We'll deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in view of your position, your post, the anti-aircraft defence for all of Kosovo, you had daily information about NATO attacks while you were there. Did you have such information or did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: We did. From time to time, depending on the situation on the ground. Sometimes we had communications or did not have communications with our subordinates and superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for Djakovica, since you were there and you were the commander of the garrison, could you personally see for yourself what places had been hit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: For the town of Djakovica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You could see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes. I could see it myself, and we can prove it on the basis of documentation that my observers of the airspace saw, and also what we had reconnoitred before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is this a map that shows NATO operations in the area of the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the map that's been on the overhead -- on the board. Obviously it's going to be important for me to have a copy of it if I am to check its reliability, if I even have the potential to do so in time. I don't know how quickly we can get copies of these done. It's unfortunate that such an important exhibit, if it turns out to be important, comes without copies available for us. It is, of course, the accused's responsibility to have it copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was just going to inquire about that. Would the Registry be able to assist in making copies of this? Well, we'll inquire, Mr. Nice. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, General, whether -- well, it's for you to say, actually, whether it would be more visible if it were placed on the overhead projector. Is it better to view it that way or on the easel, because it has to do with the town of Djakovica only.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: We can try, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it can be moved elsewhere perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us give a number to the one that we just saw.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D321, tab 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, did the previous map receive a number, with the exact places that were bombed in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We gave a new tab number following the last tab. So it was given the number tab 47 of this binder.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 46 was the other map, with the exact places that were bombed? 46, tab 46? Has that been admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we did 46. Court deputy, can you tell us? We haven't yet admitted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm asking for it to be admitted into evidence, tab 46, the map there, that is to say all the places that were hit by NATO Air Force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As for these maps, we need translations for all the legends and explanations. So we'll mark them for identification pending that translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you also seeking admission of tab 3?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, certainly. Tab 3, and tab 46, and now you've said that this is a new tab, tab 47. So all maps. All the maps that I placed on the easel, I'm asking for them all to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the significance of tab 3? It didn't seem to relate to the question of identifying areas bombed by NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Actually, the witness didn't deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 3 contains tables in the upper left-hand corner, a detail of Djakovica, and tables on the attacks in that area, what could not be displayed on the map because the numbers are enormous. I think that General Djosan explained that, and he showed you the intensity of the attacks, the tables, the numbers, et cetera. So all that information is contained on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I at the moment have no idea what tab 3 is supposed to demonstrate, and I have no recollection of the witness saying anything about the numbers which appear on it. All I remember is him saying that it could deal -- he could deal in more detail about attacks on Djakovica, but you haven't asked him anything about that so far.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When explaining that map, he showed all of those tables in the rectangles and where you can see the number of attacks, the intensity of the attacks, et cetera, using a map of Kosovo and Metohija, where you can see the deployment of his forces. And the tables show the intensity of the attacks and the number of bombs that were used -- or, rather, the number of airstrikes. All of that can be seen on those tables, and that is precisely what he indicated. If you look at the transcript, I'm sure that you'll find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am looking at the transcript, and if you can assist me to identify the point, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can ask General Djosan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of tables are contained on the map in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There seems to be confusion. Some have recollection of and I have none, and I'd like to be -- I don't want the answers again, I want to see the answers he gave already, but I can't see them. If someone can help me to identify where on this transcript he deals with the tables on tab 3, then I'd like to read it. Mr. Kay may be able to help, I don't know. I made a particular note at the time that nothing of any relevance was taken from this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 3 was referred to but not dealt with is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Only the position of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Only the position of the FRY forces, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, not actually dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, put the question to the witness in relation to tab 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the question. The answer was no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the registrar to give him the table. I gave my own copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, is that the map from tab 3?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: That's the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explained something in relation to these tables. Could you please explain every table.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: The upper table, the upper right-hand table, indicates the number of attacks according to the type of building. It says "The total number of buildings, the number of attacks, damaged buildings, destroyed buildings." So the number of attacks and the effect of these attacks. Now, this is subdivided according to the type of building. First is industrial facilities and then power production, then infrastructure, and so on. And then there's the total number. So this indicates all the buildings, the facilities that were hit. Not every rocket hit a soldier, and not every bomb hit a column. So it was towns that were hit the most, and different settlements. And of course within these populated areas, a great many civilians were killed. This table here shows the increase of NATO forces from the beginning of the aggression up to the end, and it shows how it developed. Sometimes there were even 500 attacks per day at various facilities. This is according to weeks. So it is from the 24th of March until the 30th of March. There were 300 attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, and further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The 31st of what?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 30th of March.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: There were 200 attacks on the 30th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic and General, the interpreters are asking you to speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this is very important for the question that you had put in order for things to be clearer to you. If in a small area like Kosovo, already on the first day, the 24th of March, you have 300 attacks, and then 200 attacks on the next day, then I assume that this does have an effect on the civilian population in the broader area. Five hundred attacks. An attack is not just one bomb. An attack implies a large number of bombs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, an attack can be successful or unsuccessful. There were attacks that did actually hit a building or a soldier or a civilian, and there were attacks that did not hit anybody or anything. So specifically in my reports, I referred primarily to those attacks when there were effects, specifically in Djakovica. Every day, every night there was some kind of firing. Most often they would hit nothing. Sometimes they would hit a particular facility or a soldier, or sometimes a civilian, sometimes a house, sometimes the bridge, and so on. So that's what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, when you say that on one day there were 200 attacks, does that mean that on at least 200 separate occasions a NATO attacking aircraft dropped a bomb successfully, struck something significant on that one day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm confused, so perhaps you could clarify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When there is an attack, then an aircraft drops something lethal. If this falls into a forest where there are no soldiers or policemen or civilians or buildings, this is still an attack, but it doesn't mean that at that point in time there was any effect of that attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, except that you did say, "Specifically in my reports I referred primarily to those attacks when there were effects," and what I was deducing from that was that when you give a figure of 200 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- when you give a figure of 200, that's a minimum figure. There must have been on that particular day at least 200 occasions when a NATO attacking aircraft actually did something by bombing. It may have been unsuccessful because it landed in the forest, but it may have been successful, but that's what you're saying: On at least 200 occasions on that one day an attack was mounted by NATO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This table here is not a table that pertains only to Djakovo -- Djakovica or only Kosovo and Metohija. This table pertains to all of Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, this table here. This table pertains to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Just one moment, though, 'til I go back a little. You gave evidence that on the 30th of March there were 200 attacks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In the period from the 24th of March until the 30th of March. So this is according to weeks. Increase of NATO forces by weeks of attack. So this is the week from the 24th of March until the 30th of March. That was the number of attacks during that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Well, your evidence on that was that from the 24th of March until the 30th there were 300 attacks, and then you were asked some more questions, and you went on to say, and I'm quoting exactly your words as translated: "There were 200 attacks on the 30th of March," and that led me to raise the various questions I've raised. So are you now trying to tell me that that is not your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said, that this is a table according to weeks. That's the table. From the 24th of March until the 30th of March. In that week there were 300 attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A bit more, as we can see on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So should I regard you as withdrawing the answer that there were 200 attacks on the 30th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to hear when I said that. Where did I say that, that on that day there were that many attacks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you said it this morning. It's here in front of me. But can I take it that that's wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it was a slip of the tongue, because all of this is by weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. It's a simple --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a simple question: Is it wrong to say that there were 200 attacks on the 30th of March? Is that inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd have to calculate that. I would have to do the arithmetic involved. Perhaps that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it may be right. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let us admit, then, that map. We'll mark it for identification pending translation. And tab 2 as well. That's the book. His book, yes. And then we'll take the adjournment now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, what else do we find on that map as far as tables are concerned? Could you read it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: We see an overview of registered sorties of the combat aviation by countries involved and an overview of lethal weapons, projectiles used, and we can see Djakovica specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do we see on that specific Djakovica map?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: We see the number of buildings that were targeted, where it says 18 per cent were on the territory of Djakovica. And we see the buildings that were targeted during these attacks. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So specific attacks and the number of attacks per building or feature. Number of features, number of attacks per feature. As I said, the number of features, number of attacks per feature, and features that were targeted with the number of attacks per feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many strikes were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: 236 strikes on 38 features.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the number of bombs and projectiles is larger than those numbers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Depending on the type of plane and the type of weapon it carries, the number of projectiles is always higher. There were 12 strikes on the town itself, and then on the barracks, Devet Jugovica barracks, which was in the centre, there were 13 strikes. Cabrat feature, 46 strikes. Installations of the reserve, 28 strikes. All this is in the centre of Djakovica. Furthermore, we see strikes in the border area Brovina, Batusa, Molici, each of them six times, one of them 18 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, General. You showed us on the map all places that were targeted by the NATO aviation, and I read out to you a list of towns mentioned in paragraph 63 where some sort of deportation is claimed. According to your assessment and from what we see on the map, was the density of targets large in all those places?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Sometimes it's higher, sometimes it's lower. In Vucitrn, for instance, it was lower, whereas Djakovica, Prizren, Pristina, Urosevac, Pec, Decani, the density of strikes was extremely high.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that in Vucitrn the density of strikes was lower, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Well, the town of Vucitrn is small, and that's why, relatively speaking, there were less strikes against it. You can also calculate it on the basis of number of strikes per square kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I read out to you all the places from which there was alleged deportation. Did you show us all of them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, all of them. Urosevac was hit many times, the town and its suburbs. Gnjilane, Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We won't go back to all those places.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's the point, Mr. Robinson. It transpires that, according to paragraph 64, our forces are charged with deportation only from those places that were bombed. There seem to be no deportation from other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... accused is going to give evidence, he should be restrained from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I know it's a comment, and we'll treat it that way, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, it is alleged that on the 24th of March, 1999, the old mosque in Rogovo, Bazar mosque, Hadum and the Islamic library next to it were among cultural facilities that were partially or completely destroyed. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: That is not true. The first rocket fell on Djakovica at 2000 hours. My operations duty officer received a report from a MUP unit that the centre of the town was hit. I was at Cabrat at the time, which is a hill overlooking Djakovica from which you can see the town as on the palm of your hand. Since we had equipment that was not suited for night action, we were mainly located in our shelters. After several detonations, I saw from that hill that the Catholic street where the said mosque was located was on fire. The mobile post of the brigade was next to Marsenica house, next to the hill itself, in a sheltered place at the foot of the hill. That is the truth that I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So according to what you say, there was no activity on the part of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that only the NATO aviation was active that night.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: That night there was only action by the NATO Air Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It is also said that: "From the 2nd to the 4th of April, 1999, thousands of Kosovo Albanians living in the town of Djakovica and neighbouring villages joined a large convoy, either on foot or driving in cars, trucks, and tractors, and moved to the border of Albania." What do you know about that? What would be the reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 63(h)(i) may be right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 63(h)(i). Then Djakovica is also mentioned in (ii).

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, General, below that map is the map we discussed before we reached tab 3, the one that you explained a moment ago. That one relates only to Djakovica. It is still up there, although in the meantime we had returned to tab 3. So we haven't looked at it at all.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's my impression, General, that the format of that map is much smaller, and maybe it would be better to put it on the overhead projector, because we can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the overhead projector, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it's not included in this binder?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not. It's a map that has just been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does that map show, General? It's only Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: This map shows NATO action in the area of defence of the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Brigade that was in the area of Djakovica. So it's in this area where Djakovica is. And the map shows the places and activities of NATO aviation by type of weapon used and by period. According to the same principle, from the 24th of March until the 25th of May, from the 26th of April until the 24th of May, and from the 25th of May until the end. That's how we distinguish between periods; by colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explain that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: The orange -- orange depicts action of NATO aviation from the 24th of March until the 25th of April. So it includes the first day. Blue shows the period from the 26th of April to the 24th of May. As for lethal charges or weapons, the arrows show rockets. This diamond shows one type of bomb, the circle shows a cluster bomb, this shows fluorescent bombs, and the small triangle shows depleted uranium, and this little truck shows action or strikes on refugee columns, and the last symbol shows strikes on settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Columns or settlements?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: A column was in Meja, and a settlement was in Bistrazin. From this map we see that in the first month, until the 24th of April, there were several strikes on the town of Djakovica, on features around Djakovica, including the Devet Jugovica barracks, and several features in the vicinity of Djakovica in the direction of the border. We also see that, as time went on during the aggression, the number of weapons increased, but it is typical that cluster bombs, regular bombs, and rockets were used all the time, and only depleted uranium was used solely in the later period. All this information can be found in war logs and combat reports, and we can take this as detailed, accurate information. If, for instance, there was a break in communication and we were unable to inform the corps command, which was in Pristina, in such cases we were unable to report certain incidents of action, certain strikes, at press conferences. This was particularly due to the fact that there were many repeaters in this area, many towers and communication equipment. This is, generally speaking, the area of responsibility of the 549th Brigade, where my brigade command was also located. We can also see on the map which features were targeted and how the intensity grew. With the attempt to break through the line, the defence line at Kosare, a large number of NATO planes carrying cluster bombs were used, and that can be considered as support to the forces that were trying to break into the territory of our state from the area of Kosare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you have explained the intensity of action, the density of strikes in particular places from which refugees fled. So what is your conclusion about the main reason why people fled?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: My basic conclusion is that refugees started leaving in order to flee NATO action but also -- but especially in the area of Djakovica, also fearing that they might be trapped in an area where forces of our country, the army, and the MUP would clash with the terrorists. Plus, as I said, there was propaganda. There were threats. There were people who were forced to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The opposite side claims that the forces of the FRY and Serbia directed people to go in certain directions and then at the border took away identity papers and licence plates from the people who were fleeing. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: As for direction, the direction was set by the NATO aviation. It was perfectly logical that people from Djakovica would go across the Fatucit [phoen] pass, taking the shortest route to safety. It was also normal that people from Prizren would go via Grbica, that people from Urosevac would go via Kacanik. So it was NATO action that determined who would be going where. Everybody took the shortest route to safety. As for your second question, there was not a single incident that I know of or that was reported to me where our army, our security forces, would be taking people's identity papers. Why would they do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 65(ii), it says that the forces --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have a reference, please, to the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, Mr. Milosevic. The interpreter would like an accurate reference. It's paragraph 65 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: More likely to be 63, again, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what subparagraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (ii). (k)(ii). No, wait a minute. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's (h).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's (h)(ii).

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It is (h)(ii), subparagraph (ii). We have (h), then (h)(i), and then (h)(ii), et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "... the forces of FRY and Serbia launched a massive attack against the Carragojs, Erenik and Trava valleys (Djakovica municipality), including the remaining residents of the aforementioned villages, in order to drive the population out of the area."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: That's not true. The Carragojs valley is in the border belt, rear border belt, between the communication lines of Korenica, Ibrovina [phoen], and Junik, those roads, and another communication line, Djakovica-Pec. And it is very important -- a very important area. There's a lot of forest, wooded area, and it was a stronghold, a very strong stronghold of the terrorist forces. At that time, there was the danger looming that these terrorist forces would be support and reinforcement to the forces which would come from Kosova, penetrating into our territory. And on the other side, they prevented -- on the other hand, they prevented supplies from coming in to our forces who were fighting the terrorists in the area of Kosare, Morina, Batusa, and so on and so forth. In order to avoid this situation and avoid holding our forces under siege, and at the time there was great support from NATO -- the NATO Air Force at the Kosare area, the corps command took the decision to neutralise the terrorists. Before that, in that same area, we had a number of conflicts and clashes between the terrorists and the forces of the police and army, and there were also attacks launched against the civilian population. So there was absolutely no question of the fact that the army of Yugoslavia, or as it says here the forces of the FRY and Serbia, that they launched an offensive. Quite the contrary. It was an anti-terrorist operation aimed at weakening the enemy forces which were concentrated at that location during that period of time, where there were three brigades of the Siptar terrorists. And there was great danger that they would, in a way, be a descent axis for the ground forces which might have succeeded in reaching Kosare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But in the same paragraph that I mentioned, it says: "In Meja, Korenica, and Meja Orize, a large, and as yet undetermined, number of Kosovo Albanian civilian males were separated from the mass of fleeing villagers, abducted and executed. Throughout the entire day, villagers under direct threat from the forces of the FRY and Serbia left their homes and joined several convoys of refugees using tractors, horse carts, and cars, and eventually crossed into Albania." Once again, identity documents are mentioned. I don't want to ask you about that, we've already discussed that issue, but what I'm asking you now is about these people in Meja, Korenica, Meja Orize, in those places.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Meja, Meja Orize, and Korenica are located in the Crnogorac valley, and by virtue of their location, they were no less important than the valley mentioned a moment ago. On the other hand, neither I nor any of our people had any knowledge of anything untoward happening in the sense of a crime having taken place. I was the garrison commander, and I never heard at any briefing when anybody reported to me that anybody mentioned any operations or crimes there, having been committed there. And in addition to that, many of my officers from my brigade lived in Djakovica, had lived in Djakovica for ten years, in fact, and all my commanding officers were duty-bound, had the obligation to inform the commander of the brigade about all events that took place. Nobody ever informed me about anything like that nor at the briefing sessions did I ever hear from anyone that an event of that kind had ever taken place. So I don't believe it. I don't believe anything like that could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. That anything like that could have happened. Here it says: "... a large, and as yet undetermined, number of Kosovo Albanian civilian males were separated from the mass of fleeing villagers, abducted and executed."

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: That is impossible. Our army and police would certainly never do anything like that. And the second point that remains unclear: How come that it always says "civilian males"? It never mentions terrorists anywhere. The terms used are never KLA members. It is never uniformed persons, terrorists, that are referred to. It is not possible that they were only civilian males, civilians and only civilian males, and that they alone were allegedly the victims of attacks by the FRY and Serbia, or their forces. Quite simply, no mention is made of a basic fact here, and that is that we fought against terrorists. It was terrorists that we fought against. And by the by, who was it that Paddy Ashdown spoke to during the training session if they were all civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this same thing, General, is mentioned in paragraph 66, the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Can I ask, was there any bombing in that area at the time referred to in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that area along the ridges, on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the outskirts of the area there were bombings. Cabrat, for example, was bombed a maximum number of times. Then in Meja there was an attack on a refugee column. In Duzanj, in Zur, Zub, Ponosevac, on the road from Brovina to Junik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... refugee column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] NATO -- the NATO Air Force. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph -- I'm not going to repeat what it says in paragraph 63 and then is repeated in paragraph 66 about the attack on the Carragojs valley with the intention that is alleged here and which you are denying. Anyway, in that same paragraph, 66, the following is stated that: "A large number of members of the forces of FRY and Serbia were used setting up several checkpoints. Throughout the day, the villagers left their homes faced with an onslaught of FRY forces and joined up with some of the convoys of refugees on tractors, carts ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we have a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they go on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a moment. The reference to that is 66(i).

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without a doubt, there was control over the territory. There was control over the roads, and that is indeed the obligation on the part of the MUP, to control movement. That is not something that is challenged. But what I want to say is this: The army and the police never expelled anybody, nor did they influence the decision of Albanian refugees to leave. In Djakovica, I saw many columns. They weren't as large, truth to tell, as is mentioned in some media, but those columns did go on foot. There were never any males in them. For the most part, they were women and children. Now, as far as the attack in Meja is concerned, the air force strikes, I arrived there five minutes after an airstrike had taken place, and I was an eyewitness myself of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in that same paragraph it says: "In Meja, Korenica, and Meja Orize, a large, and as yet undetermined, number of Kosovo Albanian civilian males were separated from the mass of fleeing villagers and abducted. Many of these men were summarily executed, and approximately 300 persons are still missing. Identity documents pertaining to at least seven persons who were last seen at Meja ... were found on bodies exhumed from a clandestine mass grave located in Batajnica ..." What can you tell us about those allegations in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Well, that seems to me to be quite unbelievable. I explained a moment ago that the army and police never engaged in such activity. There was simply no need for them to act that way. The army and the police settled accounts with the terrorists. They clashed with the terrorists in cases where they were directly attacked by them and where they had to defend their units and positions. All the rest, and constant mention is made of this, that they were all males, that they were all civilian males, loses all meaning and sense when we know how many, just how many terrorists there were in Kosovo and Metohija. Everybody talks about them. Everybody mentions them. Everybody saw them. And it is quite inconceivable that suddenly no mention is made of the fact that these people were terrorists or KLA fighters, whichever you -- whichever way you like to put it. It always says "civilian males."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you accept, or do you have knowledge of, I think is the correct question, of bodies being exhumed from a clandestine mass grave in Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard something about that. There was -- it was rumoured, especially after 2001. However, I don't believe it, and it seems to me quite unimaginable that somebody could have done something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't believe that there was a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that it was not a mass grave. Possibly someone brought in the bodies, but I know that it is not a mass grave. I -- after Markale, I know of all the kinds of things that could be done and could happen, and I have had experience with manipulations, and I claim that they were sheer manipulations, conducted with a specific intent which I'm sure you all know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 66(e), it says that: "On the evening of the 26th of March, 1999 --" "On or about the evening of the 26th of March, 1999, in the town of Djakovica, forces of the FRY and Serbia came to a house at 134a Ymer Grezda Street. The women and children inside the house were separated from the men, and were ordered to go upstairs. The forces of the FRY and Serbia then shot and killed the six Kosovo Albanian men who were in the house." See we're dealing with the 26th of March, here, 1999. Were you in Djakovica then?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Djakovica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were the commander of the Djakovica garrison at that time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was the commander of the Djakovica garrison at that time, and I did have talks with the president of the municipality and also head of the Ministry of the Interior, and also -- well, I said that some of my officers in fact lived in Djakovica and had lived there before the beginning of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's just clarify this point. When you say "talks," did you have regular meetings? You were the garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned the mayor, the president of the municipality, and the head of the Secretariat of the Interior. Did you have any regular meetings with those leaders; civilian, police, and other leaders at the level of Djakovica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, we did have meetings from time to time when the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How frequent would that have been?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Well, two or three times a week, depending on the situation. And therefore we exchanged information, each other's information, and at no point did I receive any information to that effect which would indicate that anything like that was going on in town or had happened in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As the garrison commander, your military policemen were there. You spoke to the chief of MUP, the president of the municipality. Would you have had to have known if an event like that had taken place? You were there on the spot. Djakovica is not New York, it's a relatively small town. Would you have had to have known about it if it had happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can't be said to be free of comment. Can't be said to be free of leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, reformulate the question without comments and without leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, General. You've explained this, how often meetings were held at municipal level, that is to say the municipal leaders and the garrison commander. Could something like that have happened without you knowing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: No. That could not have happened. Something like that could not have happened without me knowing about it, learning about it from the head of the municipality, or from the chief of police of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 66(h) it says that: "On or about the late evening of the 1st of April, 1999, and continuing through the early morning hours of the 2nd of April, 1999, the forces of the FRY and Serbia launched an operation against the Qerim district of Djakovica. Over a period of several hours, forces of the FRY and Serbia forcibly entered houses of Kosovo Albanians in the Qerim district, killed the occupants, and then set fire to the buildings." Where were you on the 1st and 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: On the 1st and 2nd of April I was in that area. I was in Djakovica but I was in Ljug Bunar, in that neighbourhood, which is right next to Qerim. Ljug Bunar cannot be reached without going through Qerim. As for the night in question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 1st of April and the early morning hours of the 2nd of April; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: That night one of my radars was hit and two of my soldiers were killed, Simbaljevic Djordje and Ivanovic Zoran. We spent the entire night, most of us did, over there, trying to save the soldiers and to extinguish the fire on the radar. I was there myself. That night a medical team came from the town of Djakovica, also fire fighters, and all of them have to go through Qerim on their way there. I had a unit of mine there, platoon size, that was at the winery here right behind Qerim. It's at an elevation, and they can see everything from there. All of them stated that on that night they did not notice anything. So the road had not been blocked. Truth to tell, there was no electricity in town, nothing could be seen, but they didn't hear anything either. I have no knowledge whatsoever about this from relevant sources. Nobody informed me about this. Nobody reported to me about this, and I would have had to know had this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've said just now that you'd have to go through this neighbourhood of Qerim that is mentioned here in order to get to Ljug Bunar, the neighbourhood that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between Ljug Bunar and Qerim?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Five hundred metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were 500 metres away from the place where it is alleged that buildings were entered and residents were killed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was 500 metres away. This is the airport. That's what it's called. And it is actually a continuation of the Qerim neighbourhood. It's called Ljug Bunar, and that's where I was that night, on I saw what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So from this 500 metre distance, could you see somebody shooting, torching houses in Qerim, whatever?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: Quite certainly shooting and torching could have been heard from that spot, but that night all of those who were with us, and there were quite a few of us there when we were trying to save the radars, they all stated that they heard nothing. I didn't hear anything either until I read about this in Natasa Kandic's book. "Crimes in Kosovo," that's the name of the book, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Twice you've said the same thing, that everyone there said they heard nothing. When was it that everyone was expressing a view about hearing nothing that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I read this information or, rather, when the commission that was established for investigating the alleged crimes, when they called me to ask me about that, then I called my subordinates, officers who were also there, because I hadn't seen anything or heard anything. I asked them whether they knew anything about it, and they all stated that they knew nothing. Lieutenant Colonel Odak, among others, said so, commander of a battalion. Then Colonel Vukasinovic, who was commander of that unit from which these killed soldiers came and also whose soldiers were in that winery. When I said "everybody," I was actually referring to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which commission are you referring to this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commission that was established in order to clarify matters after the book was published. The book called "Kosovo: As Seen, As Told." I think that's the name of the book. That was the first time I heard about this alleged crime. Of course, I did mind, and the commission called me to ask me about this. I reacted after that. I called my own officers who could have known had this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please confine yourself to answering the questions I'm asking. The commission was established by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who established the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who were the members of the commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that members of that commission were people for the most part who were professors, doctors, experts from different fields. From the military there were responsible officers, then retired officers, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you tell me when it was established?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second, please come closer to the microphone and speak into the microphone. It's a request from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally do not know when this commission was established, but I know when they invited me to come. They invited me to come when the book came out. That was in 2001 or something like that. I think it was the end of 2001. I think. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just finally, can I take it that on the night in question there is no question of there being terrorists located in houses in Qerim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know on the basis of what you make that assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying -- well, I made the assumption on the basis that you said there was no information about any activity leading to deaths in Qerim, but perhaps I've misunderstood you. Are you saying that perhaps there were people killed in Qerim and perhaps these people were terrorists, or are you saying there was no activity there at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that I did not have any knowledge of anything having happened in Qerim. I did not say that there were terrorists there. I did not say that any such thing happened. I said that I had no knowledge until I read this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's why I asked the question the way I did, which was, if I can repeat it: Can I take it that on the night in question there is no question of there being terrorists located in houses in Qerim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say anything about whether there were or whether there were not or whether that happened. I don't want to engage in guesswork. I'm just saying what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought from the way in which you were answering questions, in view of all the discussions we've been told that you had, that if there had been terrorists in Qerim, you would have known about it, but am I wrong about that now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that I would have known had there been any terrorists. I said that I would have known about this event having happened. Of course I did not know where each and every terrorist was, where every particular terrorist was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, as for the commission you told Judge Bonomy about, is it not the Commission for the Cooperation with the ICTY? Are you referring to a different --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in that same paragraph, that is 66(h), it says that: "Tens of houses were destroyed and dozens of people were killed. For example, in Milos Gilic Street, number 57, forces of the FRY and Serbia shot the occupants and then set the house on fire. As a result of the shooting and the fire set by the forces of the FRY and Serbia at this single location, 20 Kosovo Albanians were killed. Of whom 19 were women and children." What is your knowledge about this particular event?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DJOSAN
utterances.text: In response to that, I could answer the same way I did about Qerim: Had this happened, I would have known about it. As for this, no one informed me about it. No one reported to me about this, and I did not have any knowledge about this, nor do I believe that this happened until I read it in the book that you were talking about. So I certainly would have known had it happened. Somebody would have informed me about this. After all, in the unit we had officers who lived in Djakovica and they would have known. I was absent often from Djakovica because I had units throughout the area of Kosovo and Metohija, but my other organs were there, and they were also responsible and they would be duty-bound to react to any event that they knew of had something like this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In paragraph 105, it says: "In addition to the forced expulsions of Kosovo Albanians, forces of the FRY and Serbia also engaged in a number of killings of Kosovo Albanians since the 24th of March, 1999.
